raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old male with no past medical history presented with an occipital headache for 10 days. It was associated with fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, somnolence and difficulty walking. He denied focal weakness, paresthesia, neck stiffness, visual changes, chest pain, shortness of breath, urinary and bowel incontinence. The patient was in a monogamous heterosexual relationship. He endorsed a history of social drinking but denied smoking or drug abuse. Medication history was unremarkable.
The patient was afebrile with a heart rate of 88 bpm, RR 21/min, and BP 136/97 mmHg. Physical exam was unremarkable except for pallor and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Labs were significant for hypotonic hyponatremia and normal complete blood count (CBC). Computed tomography (CT) scan head without contrast showed ex vacuo dilatation of the left lateral ventricle (Figure 1).
Lumbar puncture was done and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis unveiled cryptococcal meningitis. Multifocal nodularities involving bilateral basal ganglia consistent with cryptococcomas, were present on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), along with leptomeningeal enhancement and chronic lacunar infarcts. Induction chemotherapy was started with amphotericin and flucytosine.
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis reported diffuse mediastinal, retroperitoneal, inguinal lymphadenopathy with splenomegaly. Immunodeficiency workup revealed a CD4 count of 208 muL-1. HIV testing, serum protein electrophoresis, serum light chains and quantitative immunoglobulins were non-diagnostic. CD4 lymphopenia was attributed to acute infection and the patient was sent to a nursing home for two weeks of IV amphotericin therapy. However, he had persistently low absolute CD4 count ranging between 161 and 213 muL-1 on outpatient follow-up.
Three serial lymph node biopsies for etiological workup of CD4 lymphopenia were nonconclusive, revealing a normal analytic cytometric immunophenotypic analysis. A bone marrow biopsy with immunophenotypic and cytogenetic studies (including karyotype, BCR/ABL1, JAK2 V617F, exon 12 mutations, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) for platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGRF) alpha, beta, and fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1)) was normal. IgH gene rearrangement studies showed a weak peak on B cell framework III on repeat assays, not strong enough to be termed as monoclonal. T cell receptor (TCR) gamma gene arrangement did not point towards a definite diagnosis. Moreover, a review of the sample by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) also proved to be inconclusive. The patient was hence labeled as a case of idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia.
After management of acute meningitis, he was discharged on fluconazole and augmentin therapy. The patient had a stable CD4 count without features of any immunodeficiency-related illness on the subsequent outpatient visits but was lost to follow up after three months of initial presentation. Attempts to contact the patient were unsuccessful, however, emergency contact (friend) revealed that he returned to India and was hospitalized for rapidly progressive dyspnea and confusion. He later died of multiorgan failure after 15 days of MICU stay.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 10-day history of occipital headache accompanied by fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, somnolence, and gait difficulty.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 10 days prior to admission, the patient developed a persistent occipital headache associated with fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, dysarthria, somnolence, and difficulty walking.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history; monogamous heterosexual relationship; social alcohol drinker, non-smoker, and no illicit drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for occipital headache, fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, somnolence, and difficulty walking. Negative for focal limb weakness, paresthesia, neck stiffness, visual changes, chest pain, dyspnea, or bowel/bladder incontinence. No home medications.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: afebrile, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min, blood pressure 136/97 mmHg. Physical examination was unremarkable except for pallor and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Hypotonic hyponatremia with a normal complete blood count; HIV testing, serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, and quantitative immunoglobulins were negative/normal.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was persistently low at 208/uL (ranging 161-213/uL on outpatient follow-up). Non-contrast head CT showed ex vacuo left lateral ventricular dilatation; brain MRI demonstrated multifocal bilateral basal ganglia nodularities consistent with cryptococcomas, leptomeningeal enhancement, and chronic lacunar infarcts; lumbar puncture CSF analysis confirmed cryptococcal meningitis. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis showed diffuse mediastinal, retroperitoneal, and inguinal lymphadenopathy with splenomegaly; three serial lymph node biopsies and a comprehensive bone marrow biopsy (flow cytometry, karyotype, BCR/ABL1, JAK2, PDGFR, FGFR1, IgH/TCR gene rearrangements, and NIH review) were non-malignant and inconclusive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis and bilateral basal ganglia cryptococcomas associated with idiopathic CD4+ T-lymphocytopenia (CD4 161-213/uL), confirmed by CSF analysis and brain MRI alongside exclusion of HIV and hematologic malignancy via three lymph node biopsies and bone marrow molecular/cytogenetic workup. Treated with induction IV amphotericin B (including 2 weeks at a skilled nursing facility) and flucytosine followed by discharge on oral fluconazole and amoxicillin-clavulanate; he remained stable for 3 months before returning to India, where he was hospitalized with rapidly progressive dyspnea and confusion and died of multiorgan failure after 15 days in the MICU.
